<reason>Side B wins by exposing that Side A's case collapses into circularity. In Rebuttal 2, Side A concedes that scrutiny requires proof of confidential data pooling, adherence discipline, and commitment—the very elements that constitute direct coordination. Side B demonstrates that this either makes the proposition redundant (if those facts are already proven, existing law applies) or overbroad (if it applies to all users of shared tools regardless of design). Side B also lands a decisive blow on the burden-shifting proposal, showing that treating category use "as if coordinating directly" presumes guilt before evidence and imposes disproportionate costs on small landlords. While Side A builds a compelling functionalist narrative, Side B successfully argues that the proposition as written sweeps in innocent forecasting tools and fails to bridge the gap between shared software and shared agreement.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (A1/A2), where they catch Side A retreating to an evidence-based test (confidential pooling + adherence discipline) and expose the circular reasoning: using a cartel presumption to discover agreement, then citing that agreement to justify the presumption. This neutralizes Side A's core path to victory.</best_rebuttal>
